concepts.name: Constitutional Position of High Courts: Articles 214–231
key_dimensions: Article 214 — one High Court per state (vs. exceptions under Article 231 for common HCs)
Parliament's power to establish a common High Court for two or more states
Existing HCs at commencement of Constitution vs. newly created ones
UPSC trap: HC is a constitutional court, not a statutory court — implications for its powers

concepts.name: Original Jurisdiction of High Courts
key_dimensions: Article 225 — existing jurisdiction preserved; original jurisdiction in matters of admiralty, matrimonial, probate, contempt
Distinction between original civil jurisdiction (e.g., Calcutta, Bombay, Madras HCs) and ordinary HCs
Original jurisdiction in election petitions under Representation of the People Act, 1951
UPSC trap: Not all HCs have original civil jurisdiction — only the 3 Charter High Courts do

concepts.name: Appellate Jurisdiction of High Courts: Civil and Criminal
key_dimensions: Civil appellate jurisdiction — appeals from subordinate courts under CPC and special statutes
Criminal appellate jurisdiction — appeals from Sessions Courts, conviction with 7+ years imprisonment
First appeal vs. second appeal distinction and grounds of interference
UPSC trap: HC cannot ordinarily interfere with concurrent findings of fact in second appeal — only questions of law

concepts.name: Writ Jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226
key_dimensions: Article 226 vs. Article 32 — HC has wider writ jurisdiction (any purpose, not just FR enforcement)
Territorial jurisdiction: 'cause of action' test vs. seat of authority — expanded scope post-Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar
HC can issue writs against private bodies performing public functions
UPSC trap: Article 226 is not suspended during National Emergency (unlike Article 32) — a critical distinction

concepts.name: Supervisory Jurisdiction under Article 227
key_dimensions: Superintendence over all courts and tribunals within territorial jurisdiction (except military tribunals)
Distinction between Article 226 (writ jurisdiction) and Article 227 (supervisory jurisdiction) — nature and scope
Article 227 cannot be used to exercise appellate jurisdiction in disguise
UPSC trap: Article 227 extends to tribunals, whereas Article 226 writs may not lie against all tribunals equally

concepts.name: Power of Judicial Review in High Courts
key_dimensions: HC can strike down state legislation and executive actions violating Part III or Constitutional provisions
Relationship between HC judicial review and Supreme Court's power under Article 32
Doctrine of 'basic structure' — can HC apply it to constitutional amendments?
UPSC trap: HC cannot review Parliamentary legislation on the ground of violation of DPSP alone — must be FR violation

concepts.name: High Court as Court of Record under Article 215
key_dimensions: Powers of a Court of Record: judgments have evidentiary value, cannot be questioned in subordinate courts
Inherent power to punish for contempt of court — civil and criminal contempt
Contempt of Courts Act 1971 — interplay with constitutional contempt power
UPSC trap: Being a Court of Record is not the same as having original jurisdiction — common confusion

concepts.name: Contempt Jurisdiction of High Courts
key_dimensions: Article 215 — HC has power to punish contempt as a Court of Record
Civil contempt (wilful disobedience) vs. criminal contempt (scandalising court, prejudicing proceedings)
Defences available: truth as defence introduced by 2006 amendment to Contempt of Courts Act
UPSC trap: HC's contempt power extends to contempt of subordinate courts within its jurisdiction, not just itself

concepts.name: Jurisdiction over Tribunals and the HC–Tribunal Interface
key_dimensions: L. Chandra Kumar case (1997) — HC judicial review over tribunal orders is part of basic structure
Article 323A and 323B — Parliament/state legislature can exclude HC jurisdiction in favour of tribunals
Post-L. Chandra Kumar: all tribunal orders must be subject to HC scrutiny under Articles 226/227
UPSC trap: L. Chandra Kumar overruled S.P. Sampath Kumar — exclusion of HC jurisdiction is unconstitutional

concepts.name: Transfer of Cases between High Courts and Supreme Court
key_dimensions: Article 228 — HC can withdraw cases from subordinate courts if substantial question of constitutional law arises
Article 139A — SC can transfer cases from one HC to another or from HC to SC
Distinction: Article 228 is an HC power; Article 139A is an SC power
UPSC trap: Article 228 transfer to HC itself (not to SC) — the HC then disposes the case or returns it after deciding the constitutional question

concepts.name: High Court's Power of Certification under Article 132, 133, and 134A
key_dimensions: Article 134A — HC may certify a case for appeal to SC on its own motion or on application
Certificate under Article 132 (constitutional questions), 133 (civil), 134 (criminal) — different thresholds
HC has discretion to grant or refuse certificate — SC can also grant Special Leave under Article 136
UPSC trap: Certificate by HC under Article 133 requires 'substantial question of law of general importance' — not all civil cases qualify

concepts.name: Territorial Jurisdiction and Seat of High Courts
key_dimensions: Article 231 — Parliament can establish a common HC for two or more states (e.g., Punjab & Haryana HC)
Bench vs. seat of HC — concept of circuit benches and permanent benches
Issue of separate HC for a state (e.g., demand for separate HC for Telangana — resolved in 2019)
UPSC trap: The President decides the seat of the HC — not the HC itself or state government

concepts.name: Appointment, Removal, and Conditions of Service of HC Judges
key_dimensions: Article 217 — appointment by President in consultation with CJI, Chief Justice of HC, and Governor
Removal process: same as SC judges — address by both Houses + President's order (Article 217(1)(b))
Collegium system for HC appointments — Third Judges Case (1998) and NJAC judgment (2015)
UPSC trap: Governor is consulted for HC judge appointment (unlike SC where only CJI and SC judges consulted) — key distinction

concepts.name: Acting, Additional, and Retired Judges of High Courts
key_dimensions: Article 223 — appointment of Acting Chief Justice when seat is vacant or CJ is absent
Article 224 — appointment of Additional Judges (max 2 years) and Acting Judges for temporary increase in work
Article 224A — retired judges can be appointed with consent of President and the retired judge
UPSC trap: Additional judges (Article 224) cannot be confirmed as permanent judges directly — a fresh appointment is needed

concepts.name: Independence of High Courts: Salaries, Tenure, and Transfer
key_dimensions: Salaries charged to Consolidated Fund of the State (not voted — Article 229)
Transfer of HC judges by President under Article 222 — must be in consultation with CJI (binding post-Second Judges case)
Security of tenure — can be removed only by impeachment process
UPSC trap: HC judges' salaries are charged to the State's Consolidated Fund, unlike SC judges whose salaries come from the Union's Consolidated Fund

concepts.name: High Court's Jurisdiction over Election Disputes
key_dimensions: Article 329 — bar on courts (including HCs) to interfere in electoral process during elections
Post-election: election petitions lie before HC under Representation of the People Act, 1951
HC's jurisdiction to decide disputes relating to elections to state legislature and Lok Sabha from the state
UPSC trap: During election process, Article 329 bars HC writ jurisdiction — but HC can examine post-election disputes; Presidential/VP election disputes go directly to SC

concepts.name: Distinction between Article 226 (HC Writs) and Article 32 (SC Writs)
key_dimensions: Scope: Article 226 — any purpose (not limited to FR); Article 32 — only FR enforcement
Article 32 is itself a fundamental right; Article 226 is not — HC can refuse discretionarily
Territorial jurisdiction: HC can issue writs outside its territory if cause of action arises within
UPSC trap: Article 226 jurisdiction cannot be ousted by legislation (Whirlpool Corp. case) — and is not suspended during Emergency unlike Article 32

concepts.name: High Court's Jurisdiction over Subordinate Courts: Control and Inspection
key_dimensions: Article 235 — control over district courts and subordinate courts vested in HC (posting, promotion, leave)
Article 233 — appointment of district judges by Governor in consultation with HC
Distinction: appointments by Governor; control (service matters) by HC — dual authority leads to conflicts
UPSC trap: HC controls subordinate judiciary in service matters but the Governor (on HC advice) makes appointments — a nuanced division often tested

concepts.name: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in High Courts
key_dimensions: PIL maintainable under Article 226 before HC — relaxation of locus standi rule
HC PIL jurisdiction vs. SC PIL under Article 32 — both valid but SC has pan-India reach
Guidelines on PIL — Supreme Court's restrictions to prevent abuse (frivolous PILs)
UPSC trap: HC PILs cannot challenge central government actions that have no nexus with the HC's territorial jurisdiction — territorial limit still applies

concepts.name: Inherent Powers of High Courts
key_dimensions: Section 482 CrPC (now BNSS) — inherent power to prevent abuse of process and secure ends of justice
HC can quash FIRs, criminal proceedings using inherent powers — distinct from writ jurisdiction
Inherent powers are not unlimited — cannot override specific statutory provisions
UPSC trap: Inherent powers under Section 482 are powers of the HC as a superior court of record, not a constitutional power — but complement Article 226/227
